item.title: Decomposing Large-Scale React Components and Redesigning localForage State Management
item.description:
Frontend Architecture Modularization: Phase 2 Implementation Report

In long-term frontend operation, concentrating responsibilities into a single file causes delays in type inference and increases rendering overhead. This article records the design and implementation verification of “Phase 2: Modular Decomposition”, which splits SettingsView.tsx by responsibility.

Architectural Overview: Applying the Controller-View Pattern

To dismantle a single monolithic component, we separate it into a lightweight tab orchestrator (Controller) and domain-specific functional modules (View).

src/components/settings/
├── SettingsView.tsx # Controller (Tab state management, Props distribution)
├── GeneralSettingsView.tsx # General Module (User profile, localForage persistence, backup)
└── GroupManagementView.tsx # Dnd Module (@dnd-kit context, group reordering)
  • SettingsView.tsx (Controller): Functions as an entry point that holds only the tab switching state (activeSettingsTab) and relays required handlers and states to child components.
  • GeneralSettingsView.tsx (General Settings Module): Aggregates profile updates, wake-up time settings, JSON export/import, and data reset logic, managing the lifecycle of unsaved change flags (isDirty) and confirmation modals.
  • GroupManagementView.tsx (Dnd-Kit Module): Encapsulates @dnd-kit/core and @dnd-kit/sortable contexts, isolating the routine group reordering logic (handleChunkDragEnd).

Interface Design and Type Definitions

To prevent prop drilling resulting from module decomposition and to ensure type safety, data types passed between components are strictly defined.

import React from 'react';

export interface RoutineGroup {
 id: string;
 name: string;
 order: number;
}

export interface UserData {
 userName: string;
 wakeUpTime: string;
 theme: 'light' | 'dark' | 'system';
 groups: RoutineGroup[];
}

export interface BaseSettingsProps {
 userData: UserData;
 setUserData: React.Dispatch<react.setstateaction<userdata>>;
 openConfirmModal: (action: () => Promise<void>, message: string) => void;
}

export interface SettingsViewProps {
 userData: UserData;
 setUserData: React.Dispatch<react.setstateaction<userdata>>;
 soundService: {
 playBeep: () => void;
 };
 openConfirmModal: (action: () => Promise<void>, message: string) => void;
}

Component Implementation

1. Orchestrator (SettingsView.tsx)

Dedicate the controller to rendering routing and make it operate as a layout container.

import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { useTranslation } from 'react-i18next';
import { SettingsViewProps } from './types';
import { GeneralSettingsView } from './GeneralSettingsView';
import { GroupManagementView } from './GroupManagementView';

type SettingsTab = 'general' | 'groups';

export const SettingsView: React.FC<settingsviewprops> = ({
 userData,
 setUserData,
 soundService,
 openConfirmModal,
}) => {
 const { t } = useTranslation();
 const [activeTab, setActiveTab] = useState<settingstab>('general');

 return (
 <div classname="settings-container flex flex-col h-full p-4">
<header classname="settings-header flex gap-4 border-b pb-2 mb-4">
<button =="" onclick="{()" type="button"> setActiveTab('general')}
 className={`px-4 py-2 ${activeTab === 'general' ? 'border-b-2 border-blue-500 font-bold' : ''}`}
 >
 {t('settings.tabs.general')}
 </button>
<button =="" onclick="{()" type="button"> setActiveTab('groups')}
 className={`px-4 py-2 ${activeTab === 'groups' ? 'border-b-2 border-blue-500 font-bold' : ''}`}
 >
 {t('settings.tabs.groups')}
 </button>
</header>
<main classname="settings-content flex-1 overflow-y-auto">
 {activeTab === 'general' ? (
 <generalsettingsview openconfirmmodal="{openConfirmModal}" setuserdata="{setUserData}" userdata="{userData}"></generalsettingsview>
 ) : (
 <groupmanagementview openconfirmmodal="{openConfirmModal}" setuserdata="{setUserData}" userdata="{userData}"></groupmanagementview>
 )}
 </main>
</div>
 );
};

2. General Settings and localForage Persistence (GeneralSettingsView.tsx)

Controls local storage access asynchronously and executes transactional update operations to prevent data corruption.

import React, { useState, ChangeEvent } from 'react';
import { useTranslation } from 'react-i18next';
import localforage from 'localforage';
import { BaseSettingsProps, UserData } from './types';

export const GeneralSettingsView: React.FC<basesettingsprops> = ({
 userData,
 setUserData,
 openConfirmModal,
}) => {
 const { t } = useTranslation();
 const [isDirty, setIsDirty] = useState<boolean>(false);
 const [localName, setLocalName] = useState<string>(userData.userName);

 const handleNameChange = (e: ChangeEvent<htmlinputelement>) => {
 setLocalName(e.target.value);
 setIsDirty(true);
 };

 const handleSaveProfile = async () => {
 try {
 const updatedData: UserData = {
 ...userData,
 userName: localName,
 };
 await localforage.setItem('user_profile_data', updatedData);
 setUserData(updatedData);
 setIsDirty(false);
 } catch (error) {
 console.error('Failed to persist settings via localForage:', error);
 }
 };

 const handleExportData = async () => {
 const data = await localforage.getItem<userdata>('user_profile_data');
 const blob = new Blob([JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)], { type: 'application/json' });
 const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
 const a = document.createElement('a');
 a.href = url;
 a.download = `backup-${new Date().toISOString()}.json`;
 a.click();
 URL.revokeObjectURL(url);
 };

 const handleImportData = (e: ChangeEvent<htmlinputelement>) => {
 const file = e.target.files?.[0];
 if (!file) return;

 const reader = new FileReader();
 reader.onload = async (event) => {
 try {
 const content = event.target?.result as string;
 const parsed = JSON.parse(content) as UserData;
 openConfirmModal(async () => {
 await localforage.setItem('user_profile_data', parsed);
 setUserData(parsed);
 setLocalName(parsed.userName);
 setIsDirty(false);
 }, t('settings.confirm_import_overwrite'));
 } catch (err) {
 console.error('Import parse error:', err);
 }
 };
 reader.readAsText(file);
 };

 return (
 <div classname="general-settings flex flex-col gap-6 max-w-xl">
<div classname="field-group flex flex-col gap-2">
<label classname="font-medium" htmlfor="userName">
 {t('settings.profile.name')}
 </label>
<input classname="border p-2 rounded" id="userName" onchange="{handleNameChange}" type="text" value="{localName}"/>
 {isDirty && (
 <button classname="mt-2 bg-blue-600 text-white px-4 py-2 rounded self-start" onclick="{handleSaveProfile}" type="button">
 {t('common.save')}
 </button>
 )}
 </div>
<div classname="backup-controls border-t pt-4 flex gap-4">
<button classname="bg-gray-200 px-4 py-2 rounded hover:bg-gray-300" onclick="{handleExportData}" type="button">
 {t('settings.backup.export')}
 </button>
<label classname="bg-gray-200 px-4 py-2 rounded hover:bg-gray-300 cursor-pointer">
 {t('settings.backup.import')}
 <input accept=".json" classname="hidden" onchange="{handleImportData}" type="file"/>
</label>
</div>
</div>
 );
};

3. Group Management and Dnd Implementation (GroupManagementView.tsx)

Synchronizes drag-and-drop update events with the parent state, immediately reflecting order changes.

import React from 'react';
import {
 DndContext,
 closestCenter,
 KeyboardSensor,
 PointerSensor,
 useSensor,
 useSensors,
 DragEndEvent,
} from '@dnd-kit/core';
import {
 arrayMove,
 SortableContext,
 sortableKeyboardCoordinates,
 verticalListSortingStrategy,
 useSortable,
} from '@dnd-kit/sortable';
import { CSS } from '@dnd-kit/utilities';
import localforage from 'localforage';
import { BaseSettingsProps, RoutineGroup, UserData } from './types';

interface SortableItemProps {
 group: RoutineGroup;
}

const SortableItem: React.FC<sortableitemprops> = ({ group }) => {
 const { attributes, listeners, setNodeRef, transform, transition } = useSortable({ id: group.id });
 const style = {
 transform: CSS.Transform.toString(transform),
 transition,
 };

 return (
 <div classname="p-3 bg-white border border-gray-200 mb-2 rounded shadow-sm cursor-grab active:cursor-grabbing" ref="{setNodeRef}" style="{style}" {...attributes}="" {...listeners}="">
 {group.name}
 </div>
 );
};

export const GroupManagementView: React.FC<basesettingsprops> = ({
 userData,
 setUserData,
}) => {
 const sensors = useSensors(
 useSensor(PointerSensor, {
 activationConstraint: {
 distance: 5,
 },
 }),
 useSensor(KeyboardSensor, {
 coordinateGetter: sortableKeyboardCoordinates,
 })
 );

 const handleDragEnd = async (event: DragEndEvent) => {
 const { active, over } = event;
 if (!over || active.id === over.id) return;

 const oldIndex = userData.groups.findIndex((g) => g.id === active.id);
 const newIndex = userData.groups.findIndex((g) => g.id === over.id);

 const reorderedGroups = arrayMove(userData.groups, oldIndex, newIndex).map(
 (item, index) => ({ ...item, order: index })
 );

 const updatedData: UserData = {
 ...userData,
 groups: reorderedGroups,
 };

 setUserData(updatedData);
 await localforage.setItem('user_profile_data', updatedData);
 };

 return (
 <div classname="group-management-module">
<dndcontext collisiondetection="{closestCenter}" ondragend="{handleDragEnd}" sensors="{sensors}">
<sortablecontext =="" items="{userData.groups.map((g)"> g.id)} strategy={verticalListSortingStrategy}>
 <div classname="group-list">
 {userData.groups.map((group) => (
 <sortableitem group="{group}" key="{group.id}"></sortableitem>
 ))}
 </div>
</sortablecontext>
</dndcontext>
</div>
 );
};

Troubleshooting

1. Screen Scroll Interference Caused by Pointer Event Bubbling

⚠️ Symptom: During operation on mobile devices or trackpads, drag operations inside GroupManagementView interfere with parent element scroll events, causing the entire view to scroll mid-reorder.

🛠️ Solution: Explicitly apply the CSS property touch-action: none to the drag handle or target element, and configure a distance threshold (activationConstraint.distance: 5) in the sensor settings.

.group-management-module [data-sortable-handle] {
 touch-action: none;
}

2. Race Condition in Asynchronous localForage Import

⚠️ Symptom: Moving to another tab or reloading immediately after executing a settings import process causes IndexedDB to be overwritten with stale state data.

🛠️ Solution: Standardize to a synchronized flow where React state updates (setUserData) are triggered only after ensuring write completion to persistent storage (await localforage.setItem).

Verification Result Logs

Verification logs for TypeScript type checking and build consistency after decomposition.

$ npx tsc --noEmit --project tsconfig.json

$ ls -lh src/components/settings/
total 24K
-rw-r--r-- 1 runner staff 2.1K Oct 15 10:24 GeneralSettingsView.tsx
-rw-r--r-- 1 runner staff 2.8K Oct 15 10:24 GroupManagementView.tsx
-rw-r--r-- 1 runner staff 1.4K Oct 15 10:24 SettingsView.tsx
-rw-r--r-- 1 runner staff 680B Oct 15 10:24 types.ts

$ npm run build

> client@1.0.0 build
> vite build

vite v5.4.8 building for production...
✓ 42 modules transformed.
dist/assets/index-D7K9xQ1a.css 4.12 kB │ gzip: 1.20 kB
dist/assets/index-C8L9zP2b.js 142.80 kB │ gzip: 46.12 kB
✓ built in 420ms

Operational Notes

  • Reduction in File Line Count: Down from the original 1,683 lines, each file now stays under 300 lines (with the controller under 100 lines), significantly lowering the cognitive load of individual files.
  • Preservation of Translation Keys: Re-declaring useTranslation within each sub-module prevents missing translation context propagation and fully maintains existing i18n keys (settings.*) defined in Phase 1.
  • State Consistency Testing: Post-implementation, execute reload tests immediately after performing features that involve storage operations (profile updates, backup imports, group order changes) to confirm that actual IndexedDB data matches the UI display.</react.setstateaction</react.setstateaction

item.title: Implementation of Migration to a Stateless JWT Authentication Infrastructure in Spring Boot and React
item.description:
Building a Scalable Authentication Infrastructure in Modern Web Applications: Migration Strategy from Session-Based to JWT

In the scalability of modern web applications, the authentication and authorization architecture is a critical pillar that goes beyond mere security requirements to dictate system availability and operational stability. In a decoupled architecture combining a Spring Boot REST API and a React SPA (Single Page Application), strategies for authentication state management, token expiration, and silent refresh directly impact system resilience.

This article describes the technical details of the process undertaken by CORNERSTONE (cornerstone.io.kr) to migrate from a traditional stateful server-side session model to a stateless JWT model utilizing dual-token rotation (Access/Refresh Token).

Challenges of the Existing Session-Based Architecture

The system prior to migration relied on standard Spring Boot session management. As traffic increased, the following operational bottlenecks became apparent:

  • Operational load of session clustering: Horizontal scaling required the management of sticky sessions or distributed session stores via Redis, increasing infrastructure complexity.
  • Authentication inconsistency during deployment: During instance termination due to rolling updates or auto-scaling, users were unexpectedly logged out due to session synchronization delays.
  • Inconsistent error handling: The backend would sometimes return 302 redirects or 500 errors upon authentication failure, making it difficult for the SPA to programmatically distinguish between expiration and server errors.

To resolve these issues, the decision was made to migrate to a stateless JWT architecture based on priorities of reliability, security, operational convenience, and development velocity.

Target Architecture and Security Policy

The designed JWT authentication infrastructure is based on token separation, secure storage, and a standardized error contract.

Token Type Expiration Storage Location Transmission Mechanism
Access Token 15 minutes Client Memory (React) Authorization Header (Bearer)
Refresh Token 14 days HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax Cookie Cookie Header (Automatic)

Key Security Policies

  • Access Token: To prevent token theft via XSS attacks, it is not stored in localStorage but held only in memory.
  • Refresh Token: The HttpOnly attribute is applied to block access from JavaScript, and the Secure attribute is applied to allow only HTTPS communication.
  • Authorization Model: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is adopted, and by including roles as claims in the JWT payload, authorization checks can be performed without database lookups.

Backend Implementation: Spring Boot

A stateless verification process is realized through the configuration of a JwtAuthenticationFilter that extracts the token from the Authorization header for every request and validates the signature and expiration.

package io.cornerstone.security.jwt;

import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import lombok.RequiredArgsConstructor;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.util.StringUtils;
import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;

import java.io.IOException;

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class JwtAuthenticationFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

 private final JwtTokenProvider jwtTokenProvider;
 private static final String AUTHORIZATION_HEADER = "Authorization";
 private static final String BEARER_PREFIX = "Bearer ";

 @Override
 protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request, 
 HttpServletResponse response, 
 FilterChain filterChain) throws ServletException, IOException {
 
 String token = resolveAccessToken(request);

 if (StringUtils.hasText(token) && jwtTokenProvider.validateAccessToken(token)) {
 Authentication authentication = jwtTokenProvider.getAuthentication(token);
 SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(authentication);
 }

 filterChain.doFilter(request, response);
 }

 private String resolveAccessToken(HttpServletRequest request) {
 String bearerToken = request.getHeader(AUTHORIZATION_HEADER);
 if (StringUtils.hasText(bearerToken) && bearerToken.startsWith(BEARER_PREFIX)) {
 return bearerToken.substring(BEARER_PREFIX.length());
 }
 return null;
 }
}

Frontend Implementation: Concurrent Request Control via Axios Interceptors

To prevent a “refresh storm” where multiple API requests simultaneously trigger 401 errors when a token expires, a queuing mechanism was built to temporarily hold subsequent requests and execute them in bulk after token reissue.

import axios from 'axios';

const api = axios.create({
 baseURL: 'https://api.cornerstone.io.kr',
 withCredentials: true
});

let isRefreshing = false;
let failedQueue = [];

const processQueue = (error, token = null) => {
 failedQueue.forEach((prom) => {
 if (error) {
 prom.reject(error);
 } else {
 prom.resolve(token);
 }
 });
 failedQueue = [];
};

api.interceptors.response.use(
 (response) => response,
 async (error) => {
 const originalRequest = error.config;

 if (error.response?.status === 401 && !originalRequest._retry) {
 if (isRefreshing) {
 return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
 failedQueue.push({ resolve, reject });
 })
 .then((token) => {
 originalRequest.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
 return api(originalRequest);
 })
 .catch((err) => Promise.reject(err));
 }

 originalRequest._retry = true;
 isRefreshing = true;

 return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
 axios.post('https://api.cornerstone.io.kr/auth/refresh', {}, { withCredentials: true })
 .then((res) => {
 const newAccessToken = res.data.accessToken;
 // Update the in-memory token store
 originalRequest.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${newAccessToken}`;
 processQueue(null, newAccessToken);
 resolve(api(originalRequest));
 })
 .catch((err) => {
 processQueue(err, null);
 window.location.href = '/login?expired=true';
 reject(err);
 })
 .finally(() => {
 isRefreshing = false;
 });
 });
 }
 return Promise.reject(error);
 }
);

Operational Troubleshooting and Edge Cases

1. Client and Server Clock Synchronization (Clock Skew)

Validating the JWT exp claim on the client side posed a risk of infinite redirects due to discrepancies in device time settings. To avoid this, client-side pre-validation was abolished, and the design was changed to trigger only on 401 responses from the server. Additionally, a 60-second leeway (allowable error) was set on the server side to account for network latency.

2. Authentication State Sync Across Multiple Tabs

There was an issue where if a logout occurred in one tab, other tabs would continue to hold the old in-memory token. To solve this, logic was implemented to synchronize the authentication state across browser tabs using the StorageEvent API.

window.addEventListener('storage', (event) => {
 if (event.key === 'cornerstone_logout_event') {
 // Clear in-memory tokens and redirect
 window.location.href = '/login?expired=true';
 }
});

Operational Metric Improvement Results

Based on observation data for 90 days post-migration, significant improvements were confirmed in both infrastructure stability and user experience.

  • Authentication-related support tickets: Decreased from a monthly average of 32 to 11 (-65.6%)
  • Peak authentication failure rate: Improved from 3.1% to 0.9% (-2.2%p)
  • Average token reissue latency: Reduced from 240ms to 130ms (-45.8%)

Lessons Learned

In migrating from stateful sessions to stateless JWT, the most important factor is not the choice of technology itself, but the formulation of a consistent policy regarding token storage, expiration, and error handling. In particular, considering edge cases such as refresh storms caused by concurrent requests and client-side clock synchronization discrepancies during the design phase is essential for stable operation in production environments. At CORNERSTONE, by establishing a strict API contract between the frontend and backend, we were able to build a scalable and fault-tolerant authentication infrastructure.
